title: A page, or less
hook: Daf Yomi, or a slower pace; both count
tomorrow: can you pray in a language you barely read?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Torah read around and around, in one year or three. The cycle never ends. Today, the question of speed gets personal.
screen: `THE CYCLE NEVER ENDS.` → `HOW FAST IS YOURS?`

segments.voice: Listen to a page turn: a soft scrape, then a small slap as it lands. The Hebrew word daf means a page, a leaf, with a front and a back. Daf Yomi is a page of Talmud a day, the same page for everyone who keeps it. It sounds heroic. And if a page a day would break you? The tradition's answer about half a page is gentler than you might expect.
screen: `A SCRAPE, THEN A SMALL SLAP.` → `DAF: A PAGE, FRONT AND BACK.` → `AND IF HALF?`

segments.voice: Start with Rabbi Tarfon, in Pirkei Avot: it isn't on you to finish the work, but you aren't free to walk away from it either. Both halves matter. Not finishing is allowed. Stopping is the thing to avoid. Then a line from Proverbs, read by the Talmud as advice for learners: whoever gathers little by little will have more. The Talmud explains: someone who crams learning in big bundles ends up with less, and someone who gathers a little at a time ends up with more. Then it adds, almost laughing at itself, that the rabbis know this, and don't do it. So a page a day is one pace. Half a page is a pace. One line, read every morning before you check your phone, is a pace. Shammai's advice in Pirkei Avot is to make your study fixed: a set time, not a set size. What counts is coming back. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud admits the sages knew slow and steady works, and crammed anyway.
screen: `NOT YOURS TO FINISH. DON'T QUIT.` · `LITTLE BY LITTLE GROWS.` · `THE RABBIS KNOW, AND CRAM ANYWAY.` · `A SET TIME, NOT A SET SIZE.` · then, large: `ANY PACE COUNTS.`

segments.voice: Take any book, or a single sheet of paper. Turn one page slowly and listen: the scrape, the small sound as it lands. Read only the first line on the new page, then rest your hand flat on it; that line is enough for today.
screen: `TURN ONE PAGE. LISTEN.` · `ONE LINE.` · `A HAND ON THE PAGE.`

segments.voice: A page: the daf, one leaf of Talmud with its two sides, read a page a day or a line a day, as long as you keep coming back.
Something to keep: any pace counts. A line at a time, little by little, it grows. Catch you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1747 COUNTS.` → `STUDY FOR LIFE · 5 OF 15.` → `TOMORROW: CAN YOU PRAY IN A LANGUAGE YOU BARELY READ?`

howItsDone: Some Jews study a daf, a page of Talmud, every day on the shared Daf Yomi schedule; others keep a slower fixed time, a few lines or a half page, alone or with a partner.

chat.says: saba does a page of talmud a DAY. i'll be in college. if i can't keep up, why even start?
options: Start at your own pace. Little by little grows, and you don't have to finish.
Wait until after college, when you can do the full page every single day.
Only the daily page really counts. Anything slower isn't keeping up.
chat.meaning: Rabbi Tarfon: it isn't on you to finish, but don't walk away. The Talmud says little by little grows. Any pace counts.

daf.meaning: a page or leaf of the Talmud, two sides
